Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be measurable spaces with $S\ne\varnothing$, and let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Its **Dobrushin contraction coefficient** is
$$\delta(K):=\sup_{x,x'\in S}\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}},$$
where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is the event-supremum distance between probability laws in [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. Thus $0\le\delta(K)\le1$. The coefficient measures the largest total-variation separation between two one-step output laws.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

derivations.claim: Fix $x,x'\in S$ and write $p=k_x$, $q=k_{x'}$. The assumed ordered-pair bound gives $p\le Cq$ almost everywhere, so $q\ge p/C$. Where $p\le q$, $\min(p,q)=p\ge p/C$; where $p>q$, the same inequality $p\le Cq$ gives $\min(p,q)=q\ge p/C$. Hence $\int\min(p,q)\,d\lambda\ge C^{-1}\int p\,d\lambda=C^{-1}$.

Let $A_+=\{z:p(z)\ge q(z)\}$. For every measurable $A$, $|\int_A(p-q)\,d\lambda|\le\int(p-q)^+\,d\lambda$. Since $\int(p-q)=0$, the positive and negative parts have equal integral, and $\int(p-q)^+\,d\lambda=1-\int\min(p,q)\,d\lambda$; equality is attained at $A_+$. Thus [F2] gives $\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=1-\int\min(p,q)\,d\lambda\le1-C^{-1}$ by step 1.1.
The bound in step 1.2 holds for every pair $x,x'$, so taking their supremum in [F1] proves $\delta(K)\le1-C^{-1}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, all normalized weights are exactly equal and residual offspring are deterministic; in that special case put $R_t=0$. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

derivations.claim: For any bounded measurable $h$ and $s\ge1$, [F1] gives $\pi_{s-1}(E_sh)=\pi_{s-1}(k_s(\upsilon_sh))=\widetilde\pi_s(\upsilon_sh)=\pi_s(h).$ Iterating this identity yields $\pi_k(E_{k+1:t}\bar\phi)=\pi_t(\bar\phi)=0$ for every $k<t$; for $k=t$ the identity operator also gives mean zero.

Repeated application of the assumed oscillation contraction gives $\operatorname{osc}(E_{k+1:t}\bar\phi)\le\beta^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(\bar\phi)=\beta^{t-k}\Delta\phi$. By step 1.1 its $\pi_k$-mean is zero, so its infimum is at most zero and its supremum at least zero; hence its sup norm is at most its oscillation. For $k=t$ this is $\|\bar\phi\|_\infty\le\Delta\phi$.

derivations.claim: At time $0$, [F2] and the finite particle law [F7] give IID proposal particles with law $\widetilde\pi_0$. For $h\in L^1(\widetilde\pi_0)$, [F4] gives $\eta_0^N(h)\to\widetilde\pi_0(h)$. If $\phi\in L^1(\pi_0)$, then $\upsilon_0\phi$ is integrable under $\widetilde\pi_0$ and its integral is $\pi_0(\phi)$ by [F1]; also $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. Applying [F4] to numerator and denominator and dividing on the event that the denominator is positive gives $\omega_0^N(\phi)\to\pi_0(\phi)$. That event has probability tending to one because the denominator average converges to $1$.

The selected-law base at time zero follows as well. For bounded $\phi$, [F3] makes the conditional selected mean equal to $\omega_0^N(\phi)$. Under multinomial selection its conditional variance is at most $\|\phi\|_\infty^2/N$; under residual selection the deterministic floor counts have no variance and the at most $N$ remaining categorical draws give the same bound. By [F5] and step 1.1, $\check\eta_0^N(\phi)\to\pi_0(\phi)$ in probability. For integrable $\phi$, truncate at $M$. The conditional expected selected average of $|\phi|\mathbf1_{\{|\phi|>M\}}$ is its weighted empirical average by [F3], which converges to the target tail integral by step 1.1. Conditional Markov [F6], using $P(\text{tail average}>\epsilon)\le E[\min(1,\omega_0^N(\text{tail})/\epsilon)]$ and bounded continuity of $x\mapsto\min(1,x/\epsilon)$, makes the limiting tail probability vanish as $M\to\infty$. Combining with the bounded truncations proves the selected convergence for all $\pi_0$-integrable tests.

Fix $t\ge1$ and suppose the three convergences hold at $t-1$. First let $h$ be bounded. By [F2] and [F7], conditional on the selected parents, the $X_t^i$ are independent with laws $k_t(\check X_{t-1}^i,\cdot)$; measurability of $k_th$ follows from [F8]. Thus $\eta_t^N(h)-\check\eta_{t-1}^N(k_th)$ has conditional mean zero and conditional variance at most $\|h\|_\infty^2/N$. By [F5] this difference tends to zero in probability. Since $k_th$ is bounded and $\pi_{t-1}(k_th)=\widetilde\pi_t(h)$ by [F1], the induction hypothesis proves $\eta_t^N(h)\to\widetilde\pi_t(h)$.

For general $h\in L^1(\widetilde\pi_t)$, let $h_M=h\mathbf1_{\{|h|\le M\}}$. The conditional mean of $\eta_t^N(|h-h_M|)$ is $Y_N=\check\eta_{t-1}^N(k_t|h-h_M|)$, measurable by [F8]. The function inside this last empirical average is integrable under $\pi_{t-1}$ and its integral is $a_M=\widetilde\pi_t(|h-h_M|)$. The induction hypothesis gives $Y_N\to a_M$ in probability. all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$

$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$

$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. $$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$

$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$

$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$

$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$

$$\bigl\lVert E_{k+1:t}\bar\phi\bigr\rVert_\infty\le\beta^{t-k}\Delta\phi,$$

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

Fix $N\ge1$ and nonnegative input weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$. Let $p$ be the normalized probability vector, with the uniform fallback when all weights vanish, and let $C_j$ be the offspring count from [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional on the input weights, for either scheme and every $1\le j\le N$,
$$\mathbb E[C_j\mid a_1,\ldots,a_N]=Np_j.$$
This assertion concerns the counts only; it gives no variance comparison for arbitrary weights.

derivations.claim: The two child indices are independent fair draws by [F1]. They choose the same parent with probability $(1/2)^2+(1/2)^2=1/2$. The expected number of distinct parents represented is $2\{1-(1-1/2)^2\}=3/2$, since each parent is selected at least once with probability $3/4$.

If both children select one parent, identity mutation leaves two copies of that same original ancestor; all future weights remain equal because the target is unchanged. The next resampling therefore cannot restore the lost ancestor. If they select different parents, the population still contains both lineages and another independent fair resampling preserves both with probability $1/2$.

Starting from two lineages, the probability that no collapse occurs in $m$ successive resampling steps is $(1/2)^m$ by induction on $m$ using step 1.2. Hence the probability of a single represented ancestor is $1-2^{-m}\to1$, even though the expected offspring counts at each step remain $(1,1)$ by [F2].

Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, all normalized weights are exactly equal and residual offspring are deterministic; in that special case put $R_t=0$. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

For the nonnegative importance weights $w_1,\ldots,w_n$ in [[alg-self-normalized-importance-sampling]], with $n\ge1$ and at least one positive weight, define the **weight-based effective sample size** by
$$\operatorname{ESS}_w:=\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^nw_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^nw_i^2}.$$
It is a diagnostic of observed weight imbalance. It depends only on the weights, not on the integrand, proposal regions that were never sampled, or target mass outside the observed sample. It does not certify support coverage, finite variance, accuracy, or convergence.

derivations.claim: The proposal-to-target ratios are $w(A)=\pi(A)/q(A)=99/25$ and $w(B)=\pi(B)/q(B)=1/75$, and $q(A)w(A)+q(B)w(B)=1$. The event of exactly one $A$ in four IID proposal draws has probability $\binom41(1/4)(3/4)^3=27/64>0$.

The four unnormalized weights sum to $99/25+3/75=4$, so their normalized values are $99/100,1/300,1/300,1/300$. By [F2], $\operatorname{ESS}_w=\left((99/100)^2+3(1/300)^2\right)^{-1}=\frac{7500}{7351}\approx1.0203.$ The first particle carries $99\%$ of the observed weight, which explains the low ESS; the calculation concerns weight concentration only.

derivations.claim: For every pair of preceding states, both $g(x\mid x')/g(x\mid x'')$ and $q_t(x\mid x')/q_t(x\mid x'')$ equal $1$. The likelihood satisfies $0<1\le f(\ast\mid x)\le1$, and $\Delta\phi=1$. The filtering target at every $t\ge1$ has last-state law $\pi_t(X_t=1)=1/2$, while the proposal last-state law is $q_t$. Its normalized incremental Radon–Nikodym weight is $\upsilon_t(1)=1/(2\epsilon_t)$ and $\upsilon_t(0)=1/(2(1-\epsilon_t))$.

For every preceding path, the forward image of the centered test is $E_t(\phi-1/2)=\sum_{x=0}^1q_t(x\mid x_{t-1})\upsilon_t(x)(\mathbf1_{\{x=1\}}-1/2)=\sum_{x=0}^1g(x\mid x_{t-1})(\mathbf1_{\{x=1\}}-1/2)=0.$ Consequently $E_{k+1:t}(\phi-\pi_t\phi)=0$ for every $k<t$, so all earlier-time terms in [F2] vanish.

The remaining $k=t$ term in [F2] is $V_t(\phi)=\epsilon_t\left(\frac1{2\epsilon_t}\right)^2\frac14+(1-\epsilon_t)\left(\frac1{2(1-\epsilon_t)}\right)^2\frac14=\frac1{16\epsilon_t}+\frac1{16(1-\epsilon_t)}.$ Since $\epsilon_t=2^{-t-2}\downarrow0$, $V_t(\phi)\to\infty$ despite all the stated ratio, likelihood, and oscillation bounds. Thus those conditions alone do not imply the claimed time-uniform variance bound.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be measurable spaces with $S\ne\varnothing$, and let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Its **Dobrushin contraction coefficient** is
$$\delta(K):=\sup_{x,x'\in S}\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}},$$
where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is the event-supremum distance between probability laws in [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. Thus $0\le\delta(K)\le1$. The coefficient measures the largest total-variation separation between two one-step output laws.

Let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty measurable source space. Suppose a sigma-finite measure $\lambda$ on $E$ and probability densities $k_x$ satisfy $K(x,A)=\int_A k_x\,d\lambda$ for every $x\in S$ and measurable $A\subseteq E$. If $C\ge1$ and, for every $x,x'\in S$, $k_x(z)\le Ck_{x'}(z)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $z$, then the Dobrushin coefficient from [[def-dobrushin-coefficient-for-probability-kernels]] obeys
$$\delta(K)\le1-C^{-1}.$$

Let $\mathsf X$ be a nonempty standard-Borel space with a sigma-finite reference measure $\lambda$, and let $\eta_0$ be a probability on it. For $s\ge1$, supply jointly measurable, strictly positive finite densities $g_s(z\mid x)$ of probability transition kernels relative to $\lambda$, and measurable likelihood factors $f_s$ with $0<a\le f_s(z)\le b<\infty$. These specified versions satisfy, for one $C\ge1$ and every $s,x,x',z$,
$$g_s(z\mid x)\le Cg_s(z\mid x').$$
Define $c_s=\eta_{s-1}(g_sf_s)$, $\eta_s(h)=\eta_{s-1}(g_s(f_sh))/c_s$, and $E_sh(x)=g_s(f_sh)(x)/c_s$. They are the operators of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]] restricted to last-state tests in the corresponding filtering model. Put $\rho=1-C^{-2}$. For every bounded measurable real terminal test $\psi$ and $0\le k<t$,
$$\|E_{k+1:t}(\psi-\eta_t\psi)\|_\infty\le C\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(\psi).$$
For $k=t$ the identity image is bounded by $\operatorname{osc}(\psi)$; use $\rho^n=0$ for $n\ge1$ when $C=1$. This is a closed last-state-test assertion, not a contraction of arbitrary functions of the full stored path. Positivity, finiteness and the ratio bounds refer to the supplied pointwise density versions, not to unspecified unrelated null-set versions.

Use multinomial offspring resampling and the covariance $V_t$ of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]]. There is a separate filtering-density sufficient branch. Use the strictly positive finite density versions, true-transition row-ratio bound $C\ge1$, likelihood bounds $0<a\le f_s\le b<\infty$ and normalized filtering operators in [[lem-smc-centered-filtering-feynman-kac-contraction]]. derivations.claim: Every transition row is $(1/2,1/2)$, so the target and proposal transitions coincide and the likelihood contributes no correction. By [F1], $\upsilon_s=1$, hence $B=1$, and $\pi_s$ is uniform for every $s\ge0$. Since the row does not depend on its predecessor, [F2] gives $\delta(K)=0$; its density rows are identical, so [F3] also applies with $C=1$.

On the closed last-state subspace the forward operator is $E_sh_s=Kh_s$, which maps a last-state test to its uniform average. The true transition and proposal density versions relative to counting measure are all $1/2$, so [F4] applies with $C=1$, $A=1$, and $\rho=0$. No contraction of arbitrary path-history functions is asserted. The test has $\Delta\phi=1$ and is centered by $1/2$. Every earlier backward image is zero; the final $k=t$ term in the variance expansion is $\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_t}(\phi)=1/4$. Hence $V_t(\phi)=1/4$ for every $t$.

Applying [F5] with $A=B=1$, $\rho=0$ and $\Delta\phi=1$ gives $V_t(\phi)\le1$, uniformly in $t$; the exact variance $1/4$ from step 1.2 satisfies the bound. This verifies a time-uniform asymptotic-variance result under explicit mixing and weight conditions.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, all normalized weights are exactly equal and residual offspring are deterministic; in that special case put $R_t=0$. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

Use the operators and multinomial variance recursion of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]] at every selection time. For $\phi\in\Psi_t^{(d)}$, put $\bar\phi=\phi-\pi_t(\phi)$. Then
$$V_t(\phi)=\sum_{k=0}^{t}\widetilde\pi_k\!\left[\upsilon_k^2\,E_{k+1:t}(\bar\phi)E_{k+1:t}(\bar\phi)^\top\right],$$
where the $k=t$ term uses $E_{t+1:t}\bar\phi=\bar\phi$. Each summand is a finite positive-semidefinite matrix under the stated class conditions.

Fix a finite horizon $t$ and use the target/proposal flow and classes $\Phi_s^{(d)},\Psi_s^{(d)}$ of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]], with $1\in\Phi_s^{(1)}$ for every $0\le s\le t$. Run the SIR procedure with multinomial resampling at each time. For $\phi\in\Psi_t^{(d)}$, let $\omega_t^N$ be the corrected weighted empirical law and $\check\eta_t^N$ the post-resampling empirical law. Then
$$\sqrt N\{\omega_t^N(\phi)-\pi_t(\phi)\}\Rightarrow\mathcal N_d(0,V_t(\phi)),\qquad
\sqrt N\{\check\eta_t^N(\phi)-\pi_t(\phi)\}\Rightarrow\mathcal N_d(0,\widehat V_t^{\rm multi}(\phi)),$$
where $\widehat V_t^{\rm multi}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi)$. The horizon is fixed as $N\to\infty$; the theorem asserts no time-uniform finite-particle accuracy.

derivations.claim: The identity kernel leaves the uniform law invariant and has incremental weight one. Thus [F1] gives $E_{k+1:t}(\phi-\pi_t\phi)=\phi-1/2$ for every $k\le t$. Since $(\phi-1/2)^2=1/4$ everywhere, each of the $t+1$ summands in [F2] equals $1/4$. Therefore $V_t(\phi)=(t+1)/4$.

By [F3], at every fixed $t$ the weighted estimate has a valid CLT with variance $(t+1)/4$, and the post-resampling estimate has variance $(t+2)/4$. Both variance sequences are unbounded as $t$ ranges over the integers. The fixed-horizon theorem therefore supplies no uniform-in-time variance bound or finite-particle accuracy guarantee.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty measurable source space. Suppose a sigma-finite measure $\lambda$ on $E$ and probability densities $k_x$ satisfy $K(x,A)=\int_A k_x\,d\lambda$ for every $x\in S$ and measurable $A\subseteq E$. If $C\ge1$ and, for every $x,x'\in S$, $k_x(z)\le Ck_{x'}(z)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $z$, then the Dobrushin coefficient from [[def-dobrushin-coefficient-for-probability-kernels]] obeys
$$\delta(K)\le1-C^{-1}.$$

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be measurable spaces with $S\ne\varnothing$, and let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Its **Dobrushin contraction coefficient** is
$$\delta(K):=\sup_{x,x'\in S}\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}},$$
where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is the event-supremum distance between probability laws in [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. Thus $0\le\delta(K)\le1$. The coefficient measures the largest total-variation separation between two one-step output laws.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $k<t$. Define $Q_{j,t}h(x)$ by iterating the kernels $g_{j+1},\ldots,g_t$, multiplying by $f_{j+1},\ldots,f_t$, and evaluating $h$ at the final state. Put $H_{j,t}=Q_{j,t}1$ and $H_{t,t}=1$. Measurability follows from [F1], while probability normalization and the bounds on $f_s$ give $a^{t-j}\le H_{j,t}\le b^{t-j}$. Comparing the first transition row gives $H_{j,t}(x)\le C H_{j,t}(x')$ for $j<t$. Consequently $r_{k,t}:=H_{k,t}/\eta_k(H_{k,t})$ is positive, at most $C$, and has $\eta_k$-mean one.

For $j=k+1,\ldots,t$, set $L_{j,t}(x,dz)=g_j(z\mid x)f_j(z)H_{j,t}(z)\lambda(dz)/H_{j-1,t}(x)$. The recursion for $H$ shows that these are probability kernels, with strictly positive finite denominators. The ratio of two of their density rows is $[g_j(z\mid x)/g_j(z\mid x')][H_{j-1,t}(x')/H_{j-1,t}(x)]\le C^2$ by step 1.1. Thus [F3] gives $\delta(L_{j,t})\le1-C^{-2}=\rho$. Telescoping the $H$ factors in the product kernel $P_{k,t}=L_{k+1,t}\cdots L_{t,t}$ gives $P_{k,t}h=Q_{k,t}h/H_{k,t}$.

For any probability kernel $K$ and bounded real $h$ of positive oscillation, put $u=(h-\inf h)/\operatorname{osc}(h)$. Then $0\le u\le1$, and [F5] under each output law gives $K u(x)-K u(x')=\int_0^1[K(x,\{u>r\})-K(x',\{u>r\})]dr$. By [F4], its absolute value is at most $\delta(K)$. If the oscillation is zero, $K$ preserves the constant and the same oscillation bound is immediate. Hence $\operatorname{osc}(Kh)\le\delta(K)\operatorname{osc}(h)$. Iterating this inequality along the kernels in step 1.2 gives $\operatorname{osc}(P_{k,t}h)\le\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(h)$.

The filtering recursion and iterated integration [F2] yield $\eta_t h=\eta_k(Q_{k,t}h)/\eta_k(H_{k,t})$ and $\prod_{j=k+1}^tc_j=\eta_k(H_{k,t})$. Thus $E_{k+1:t}h=r_{k,t}P_{k,t}h$. Take $h=\psi-\eta_t\psi$. Then $\eta_k(r_{k,t}P_{k,t}h)=0$, and $r_{k,t}\eta_k$ is a probability by step 1.1. Therefore the global infimum of $P_{k,t}h$ is at most zero and its supremum is at least zero, so its sup norm is at most its oscillation. Step 2.1 bounds this by $\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(\psi)$; multiplying by $r_{k,t}\le C$ proves the claim. For $k=t$, the mean $\eta_t\psi$ lies between $\inf\psi$ and $\sup\psi$, giving the identity-case bound.
